AMULET:   Amulets and charms Introduction  T  he Pitt Rivers Museum has almost 6,000 amulets and charms in its collections; though not all of them are on display.
AMULET:  An amulet is defined by the Oxford English Dictionary as: ‘Anything worn about the person as a charm preventative against evil, mischief, disease, witchcraft, etc.
AMULET:  Some of the objects on display are technically not amulets or charms but objects that were used in a ritual or instilled with a supernatural power.
AMULET:   The underlying theme that unites all amulets and charms is that the people who created and used them believed in them; almost any object may become a charm or an amulet, so long as someone believes it has the power to affect or alter the world around them.
AMULET:  Some amulets and charms are examples of ‘sympathetic magic’, which generally means that the appearance of an object resembles, in some way, the cure or protection it is believed to offer.
AMULET:  Unlike some of the objects on display in this Museum, amulets and charms are still widely used in many cultures today.
AMULET:  You may have an object yourself that you trust will bring you luck! The amulets and charms on display at the Pitt Rivers Museum are material evidence of the hopes and beliefs that are shared by all of humankind.
AMULET: 278  This amulet is made from a dwarf coconut, carved with clan motifs and rubbed with lime to emphasise the design.
AMULET:  Known as marupai, such amulets are still used for magical purposes in Papua New Guinea today.

AMULET:  This amulet was worn to protect against death in battle.

AMULET:  It was used as a container for amulets and charms.
